ent position, does it occupy, then, with reference to earning powers, from the other railways? None whatever. Besides that he says it does not follow commercial lines. And yet that line from Quebec down to Moncton, which is at present a non-paying one, is to be met by competition. The people are asked to build for the Grand Trunk Pacific another line for the purpose of competing with it. The hon. minister says that the freights charged upon the Intercolonial Railway are competitive freignts against the Canadian Pacific Railway, which has a shorter line of communication. Well, then, in what position will we be when the Grand Trunk Pacific is built ? You say that that will give a shorter line from Levis to Moncton, but it will be another competing line in opposition to the Intercolonial Railway. It is time for our people to be alarmed at the position. We have statement after statement from Ministers of Railways, from one year to another, as to what the probable results will be in the future, and in that respect the present Minister of Railways differs from all his predecessors. He does not want to paint a bright future for the intercolonial Railway. He says that there is bound to be a large deficit next year unless we give him unlimited powers for the purchase of locomotives and freight cars, so that he may be able to cheapen freight rates. I suppose another necessity in that respect would be to reduce the gradients. That whole matter would involve an expenditure, not of $8,000,1X10 a year only, but greatly in excess of that amount-and for what ? For the purpose of making both ends meet. A more extraordinary statement I never heard from a Minister of Railways. The only wav, he said, to remedy the deficit is to increase the rates of freight, and he does not think he can increase them, because there is a feeling in the maritime provinces against any7 increase on account of free tolls on the canals. But he also suggests another remedy. We are, he says, short of seventy-five locomotives, and we ought to have easier grades and an increased number of freight cars ; and when we have these we will be able to carry freight cheaper and lessen the deficit. But he ought to be prepared with a financial statement showing what the expenditure in these respects will lie and how much cheaper he can carry freight if he has these improvements made. But, Mr. Chairman, it will be the same old story next year and year after year. So long as the management continues to be as it is at present, we will find a continuous record of increased deficits. There is another little detail. I see that the capital expenditure at the end of 1905 was $4,665,265 on the Intercolonial Railway. That is the capital expenditure during that year, and on the Prince Edward Island Railway it was $1,335,975. The hon minister states that the receipts of the 237 REVISE	Prince Edward Island Railway are about $11,000 less than last year, and the increase in working expenses is $65,000-Last year the deficit on that railway7 was in the neighbourhood of $90,000. Add the increased expenditure this year of $65,000 to the shortage in receipts compared with last year of $11,000, and you have $76,000 to the bad on these two items alone. The hon. minister has not given us the actual deficit or the expenditure on account of capital on the Prince Edward Island Railway, but he says that the difference between levenue and expenditure upon that road must be in the neighbourhood of nearly $90,000. Add that to the deficit of last year, and you will find that for the purpose of running a little narrow gauge road-which ought not to have cost more than $4,000,000, but on which the capital expenditure is $6,-060,000-you have a deficit ot nearly $200,000 per y7ear. What excuse can there possibly be for any such state of affairs ? 1 would say to the management of that read : If you cannot run things better, I will try something else. The hon. minister ought to have taken such a course, both on the Intercolonial Railway and the Prince Edward Island Railway, instead of coming down with that de profundis speech of his, in which he says, in the most melancholy of tones : I regret deeply to have to make such a statement. I would try some experiment, and see if the management of these roads could not be made more conducive to the interests of the people than they now are. Will the country accept such an apology 1 Will the country endorse such an exhibition of incompetency and extravagance ? I am afraid that the people do not look narrowly into the expenditure of this country. They do not criticise the enormous extravagances of the gentlemen who are our rulers at present. If they did as any commercial concern would, look into their own business more closely, the results would be very different. Here we have a Minister of Railways blandly presenting us with H statement of these two roads, showing mismanagement in every line-one of these roads 1,300 miles long and the other about 230 miles long; one a narrow gauge road, and both running through as fine a country as there is in Canada. Both are roads which ought to pay, and yet the hon. gentleman comes"down with a statement showing a deficit between revenue and expenditure of nearly $8,000,000, namely SS.OOO.OOO on the Intercolonial Railway ana on the Prince Edward Island Railway. I have not got all the figures as to the expenditure on the Prince Edward Island Railway, but I will venture to say they are between $900,000 and $1,000,000, making a deficit of $9,200,000 taken out of the pockets of the people for the purpose of running two mismanaged roads under the direction of the government. D EDITION ;

I have my duty to perform ; I have presented the facts to the people, and if the people will submit to a continuance of this mismanagement, I have toothing more to say. But it puts an end to all prospect of state-ownership of railways in this country. It is the most fatal blow that ever was struck at that policy. It shows that under the management of a government, such as now constituted, we can expect no economical management of any state concern. It puts back for fifty years in this country the prospect of state-ownership of railways or of state-ownership of any public utility. Nor do the conditions justify any such lamentable exhibition as we have had. As the Minister of Railways himself says, the government can buy materials cheaper than any other railway owner in the country. Under the system in vogue when I was manager of the Intercolonial Railway, when we invited tenders for supplies, I found that I got supplies of the best quality, because they were tested, whenever there was a dispute, by the McGill College in Montreal, whose decision was final, and we got them cheaper than any other railway in the country.
On a government railway you can get men at cheaper rates and men who will serve more faithfully than under private management. But, if you build work-shops greater than are needed, if you undertake extraordinary expenses for useless purposes from one end of the line to the other, of course you cannot look for success. When 1 ceased to have charge of the railway in 1896, I had reports from the officers who are at present in charge of the system stating that the system was in a better position than when we took charge of it. And not only was the position of the road improving, but expenditure on capital account had nearly ceased, as ought to be the case on the Intercolonial. There is no justification for expenditure on capital account on an old railway. The same is true, except for the expenditure on the branches with regard to the Prince Edward Island road. That capital account of the Intercolonial should close, as I said before. Mr. Chairman, I have set before this committee and this country the broad facts of the management of the Intercolonial; and if the people will submit to such management, they will submit to anything.

I do not intend to enter to-night into any criticism in the shape of a reply to the speech of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Emmerson). On two occasions since f entered parliament, I went through a very considerable amount of labour to analyse the annual report of the Minister of Railways of this government and to lay before the House, in some detail, the conclusions at which I arrived. But I found so little attention paid fiv hon. gentlemen opposite to any word Mr. HAGGART.
that was uttered in criticism of the government management of the Intercolonial, that I consider it would be an absolute waste of my time and of the money of this country to spend an hour in the criticism of any Minister of Railways under this administration. I say that frankly, I say it deliberately; for, having spent weeks at examination of the long and most extraordinary reports issued year after year by the government as to the management or these railways, I felt that that labour was absolutely thrown away, and time occupied in addressing the House worse than thrown away, because it involved an expense to the country. I have said before in this House that in criticising, and giving my reasons for the criticisms, that if any ordinary company in Canada or the United States, were managed as the Intercolonial is managed under this government, the directors of that railway company would be liable to criminal indictment for the manner in which the business was administered.

Oh, oh.
Mr. BARKER I say that deliberately. And I know whereof I speak. I have had some experience in railways; I have had thirty years' experience; and I say, deliberately, that if a board of directors of any ordinary railway company laid their accounts before their shareholders and the public in the way in which the accounts of the government with regard to the Intercolonial are presented, those railway directors would find themselves in jail; and I defy contradiction of that statement.
So I am not going into the details to-night. I object to going to all that labour for the third time. But the minister of Railways has made one statement in my presence to which I wish to refer. I had not intended to speak at all, but after he had made the statement to which I refer, and while sitting here at my desk, I tested the accuracy of his figures. And I will give the House the result of that test and will leave the House to judge how far they can trust accounts as explained by the hon, minister. The hon. gentleman said that the Intercolonial was 75 locomotives short of the number it ought to have for the proper conduct of its business. Am I right ?
Yes.

Well, after the hon minister made that statement 1 took the mileage and locomotives of the Intercolonial Railway and of the three other principal railways of Canada, the Canadian Pacific, the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Northern. And I found that the Intercolonial has more locomotives to the mile than any of these roads. And I will prove it. At page 1-6 of the Report of the Minister of Railways we find it stated that the Intercolonial has a mileage of 1,322 miles. And. at page I-115, of the same report, we find that the Intercolonial


I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, to be obliged again to call attention to the point to which I referred a few minutes ago, the manner in which this committee is conducted, as illustrated by what we see,-gentlemen standing up and talking all over this chamber.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

As a friend of public ownership, and as one who still at times advocates that principle in this House and elsewhere, I cannot agree with the statement made by the Minister of Railways. His statement is a very discouraging one ; and I agree with the ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Haggart) that if a better showing cannot be made in favour of public ownership, the country will not long stand what we have of it to-day. There is nothing miraculous about public ownership. Public ownership must be vindicated by a sound business administration, and by nothing else. Now have we had a sound business administration of the Intercolonial V So far as I can gather, we have had anything but that. There has been a political administration of it, there has been an extravagant administration of it, and there has been a use of it, or rather a misuse of it in the interest of other railways that happen to be rivals. Now if we are to have public ownership tried in this country, 2371
and the experiment is well worth being tried, there must be sound business administration, and good results must be shown. The road must be put into the hands of men who have no connection whatever with politics. We have seen public ownership of railways in Europe, and in every country in Europe, a budget is brought down every year containing an explanation of the state ownership of railways and its results. There is not a Minister of Railways who comes down in any of those parliaments who makes such a speech as has been made here to-night; on the contrary, he brings down a business statement, he shows his railway is being administered as a business proposition, he is showing a profit on the construction of the road, on the capital invested in the road, and he is showing that the people are getting lower and lower freight rates and a better service in every direction. Now public ownership, public administration of railways in all the countries of Europe has proved to be a success, and it is proved to be a success because it is under sound business administration and not the kind of administration we have in this country. That being the case I say we ought to make an effort to have a similar administration of our national railway. And why is not the experiment tried ? Why does not this government say : We are determined to make the experiment of a business administration of our public railway ? Let them get a man like Sir Thomas Shaughnessy, or Sir William Van Horne, or Mr. Chas. M. Hays. Let them do like the city of Glasgow, which gets a Dalrymple to administer its street railways, and the consequence is that it has the finest street railway system in the world. They are doing it in connection with telephones in the old country, they are doing it in connection with everything else, both by municipalities and by the state, and the basis of it all is that the administration is put into the hands of business men, and politics are not allowed to interfere.
Why can't we do that in this country ? Why can't we have the experiment made in public ownership by a proper administration of the railway we hav# ? It is a great railway, it is a great proposition, it could be made to pay, it could be made to pay in the maritime provinces which they say is a poor country. I agree with the hon. member for Lanark that it is a good place to try the experiment in. But let us first of all make the revenue pay the expenses, without any regard to capital account ; then let us try to pay on the capital account, and if we can do that we can extend the state system all over this country and bring great relief to the people. In Ontario we do not want to see the Intercolonial ruined, we do not wish to see it made a by-word to the people. We would like to see it prove a success in the maritime

provinces, and see it extended through Quebec and into our own province of Ontario. We would like to see the Intercolonial brought into Toronto, brought to the Niagara frontier, brought to the Detroit river, brought to the Georgian bay, and finally to the upper lakes. But we never can hope for that under such an administration as we have at the present time, and necessitating such a statement as has been made here to-night. Why, Sir, it brings the blush of shame to any one, to any citizen of this country, to hear the statement made here to-night that the railway is being run as a first-class railway with a third-class traffic, and is producing this enormous deficit that has been produced. If the character of its traffic is only that of a third or fourth-class railway, if the department is spending so much money to maintain it as a first-class railway, I want to see it maintained as a first-class railway, and I want to see it administered as a business proposition and nothing else, and as state owned railways are administered in every other country in the world. They are a success in Australia, they are a success in New Zealand. In Australia they found a Canadian railway man to take hold of and improve their system. We have got railway men in this country who can make a success of the Intercolonial to-day; we have railway men in this country who if you give them charge of that road, will make it pay running expenses out of receipts, and begin to build up a surplus against the investment on capital account. Why can't we have it ? Why cannot the Liberal party take up a proposition of this kind and show that they can do something with it ? The only thing I can see is that they have some ulterior purpose in view, they wish to discredit the principle of public ownership. We know what the Prime Minister said about public ownership in a speech made in this House when he tried to discredit the principle. Why don't they try and make it a regulator of transportation ? In the United 'States they are trying now to improve transportation by increased government regulation, and if they are not successful in that, the only thing left is government ownership and they must come to that. If they come to that in the United States it must be on the principles of a business administration, and a man like Roosevelt will take hold of the railways in that country and administer them as a business proposition, and not as a political proposition.
Now I ask the Minister of Railways to tell the people of this country why he cannot make that railway pay. If it is not paying because the freight rates are not high enough, let the freight rates be raised. No member for the maritime provinces will stand up here and justify that road being run with freight rates that don't pay. They must do either one of two things, increase the rates or reduce the expenses. I agree Mr. W. F. MAOLE'AN.
with the hon. member for Lanark that the first experiment to make is in the reduction of expenses, and in the meantime an administration on business principles instead of a political administration. I hope some effort will be made in that direction. Let them try to get feeders for that road, and make alliances that will bring business to it. But unfortunately every arrangement that has been made up to the present with other roads is in a way to milk the Intercolonial, and turn it in as a feeder to other roads instead of making other roads feeders to it. The government went into what they called a great national transcontinental system of railways, they are expending millions and millions of the people's money, but they take good care not to make the Intercolonial a part of the system. Why are we building another railway down in the maritime provinces to compete against this road we now own, when the Minister of Railways confesses there is not sufficient traffic for three ? On the contrary he should have used the Intercolonial as the basis of a thoroughly national system, and extended that system to the west and ultimately to the Pacific. But on the contrary we have given all the opportunities to a private enterprise, the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the result is that we are not having anything approaching to state ownership or a state owned railway, in this country, but the state is being bled enormously to build up great private railways which are not sufficiently cheeked nor sufficiently regulated. Now in this country we do not seem to have enough confidence in ourselves to make the experiment of a state owned railway as it ought to be made.
I deplore that fact. The hon. Minister of Finance will soon be in a position that he must justify the expenditure of state ownership we have here or be prepared to abandon it, because it is not sound financially and cannot be justified. The justification that was given here to-night as against the canal system in the west will not bear investigation. It has nothing to stand on. My hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Haggart) has dealt with that and dealt with it in a convincing way. The hon. Minister of Finance and the government will be in such a position that they cannot justify what is taking place to-day and the call will go forth for an increase in the rates and a reduction in the expenses of the Intercolonial Railway. That is the worst thing that can happen to the people in the maritime provinces. They ought to take a pride in the state owned railway. It is their servant, it is operated in their interest and they ought to take a pride in seeing that the state owned road is made a success, and that the railway is not something that ought to be milked and depleted and run in an extravagant way. Let them take an interest in having low freights, but let them take an interest in its economic and sound

business administration. If they do that they will benefit themselves and the whole country and- they will see the demand for public owned railways in this country increased. I could talk for a long while this evening in favour of state owned railways, but X do not wish (to do so. I only wish to enter 'my protest against any such statement as that made here to-night that the deficits have increased and are likely to increase. . On the contrary the statement ought to be that the prospect is that deficits are soon to end on the Intercolonial Railway and that it will not only pay its running expenses out of its traffic receipts but that it will soon be earning enough money to pay something on the investment. That is being done by all other first-class railways. whether state owned or private, and it is the only principle on which to administer a railway. You must make it a commercial success. There cannot be any other reason for the existence of a railway than that. It must be made to pay, the traffic over the road must maintain it and any proposition in favour of any o'ther kind of railway, whether state owned or not, cannot be justified. In Germany some of the railways are for the purposes of defence, but even these railways are made to work in with the commercial and business interests of the country and they are not only using them for the defence of the country but they pay from the point of view of aiding the trade of the country. In no country is the excuse made that a railway, because it is a government road, ought to be run at a loss. If the Intercolonial Railway is a round-about road why cannot it be shortened ? It is easy to make a short cut but that short cut should not be made in an extravagant way. If the Prince Edward Island Railway can be improved and they say it can be improved an expenditure should be made for that purpose, but once it has been improved the road should be run as a business proposition and its receipts should pay the cost of its maintenance. If we do that we will do something for public ownership and we will see the idea spread. I am more than discouraged to hear the statement which has been made here to-mgfit that to all intents and purposes a state owned railway cannot be made a success. What is this weakness in the Canadian people that of all the people in the worid who have an organized government they cannot succeed in the successful operation of a public owned railway ? There is very little competition. There are no railways cutting into the Intercolonial Railway except the Canadian Pacific Railway and that does not count 'in respect to local traffic at all. When we have conceived a great principle we ought to realize it and make it a success. If hon. gentlemen say that there is some kind of weakness in us as a nation, that our public men are not of the character to administer a trust of this
kind, let them say it boldly, but I repudiate that idea as a Canadian. I say that there ought to be sufficient patriotism in the men engaged in public life here to take that railway out of politics, put its administration into the hands of a commission or of one strong man who knows his business and who would have no political interference, as I would like to see it, if we did that I am sure that we would find a way of making the traffic pay the cost of maintenance. Canadians are equal to that, but the confession is now. made, as it has been made year after year in this country, that in some way a state owned railway cannot be made a success, and if that confession continues to be made I have no hope for the idea of public ownership of railways in this country. I say that public ownership is a great and growing principle. It is extending all over the world. It has justified itself in connection with railways, it has justified itself in connection with various municipal utilities and it is justifying itself in every direction today. It is a success in England, it is a success in Germany, it is a success in France, it is a success in other colonies such as Australia and New Zealand, and if it can be made a success there it can be made a success here, if we only try the experiment. Ret the government take this department absolutely out of politics. Let them provide a new administration for the Intercolonial Railway. Let this new administration be composed of smart, able railway men. Let us try that experiment for three years. Let us try it between now and the next election even if it does cost some votes in the maritime provinces. The everlasting love of office seems to be the inspiration that actuates almost all of our public men. Why do they not form an ideal and try to realize it in connection with our public affairs ? Surely ideals are better than love of office and better than votes, and if that is the case let them take the ideal of public ownership and try to realize it. If they do 1 believe the people will give them credit for it and be disposed to keep them longer in office rather than remove them. But this everlasting idea that we must not disturb this voter's interest, or the interest of that province, or else it will go against us in the next election must be got rid of. We must adopt a sound administration in connection with the Intercolonial Railway and if we do it will pay its way from this onward. Instead of having a deficit the cost of maintenance will come out of the traffic earnings and in a short time there will be a surplus which can be applied to the payment of the interest on the cost of the road.

Mr. Chairman, I want to correct a few figures I gave in reference to the expenditures on capital account and the deficit on the Intercolonial Railway. I find on looking over the report that the

amount of the expenditures on the Intercolonial Railway on capita] account for the current year was $4,214,750. Then, there is to supplement that in the supplementary estimates, $450,515. That makes a total expenditure on capital account on the Intercolonial Railway, independent of the running expenses, of $4,665,265. To this add the deficit on the Intercolonial Railway which the hon. minister says is $1,860,000, or which may be $2,000,000 at the end of the year, and it makes $6,665,265. The amount of the expenditures on capital account on the Prince Edward Island Railway last year was $1,003,300. In the supplementary estimates for this year there is a vote of $85,050, making an expenditure on capital account for the current year of $1,I'M,825 to which is to be added the deficit between the expenditure's and receipts of $200,000-I am estimating that but I think I am a good deal under the markmaking $1,335,075. I stated that the total deficit for the current year was $8,100,000 ; I find that it is $8,001,240.

I do not propose to criticise the statement of the Minister of Railways ; I do not think'it is worth criticism. The short speech of the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) was quite within the mark. I would like to draw the attention of the Minister of Finance to one phase of this matter. __It is quite true that it has always been the custom to charge the deficits of the Intercolonial Railway to capital account, but that is making a false representation to the country and making the people believe that the Intercolonial Railway is providing for itself.

speechtext: What does my hon. friend mean by saying that it has always been customary to charge the deficit to capital account ?
It has been customary.

Yes.

It is added to the capital account of the Intercolonial Railway.

speechtext: The meaning of the expression ' capital account ' in our public accounts is well known, and when the hon. gentlemen says that the Intercolonial Railway deficit is charged to capital account he is mistaken. It is charged to the general revenue of the year.
Not of the Intercolonial Railway.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The general revenue of the Intercolonial Railway is not enough. The receipts of the Intercolonial Railway are credited to the revenue of the year and the exepnditures are charged in the outlay, so that the deficit is charged against the income of the country for the year.

The deficit is made out in such a way that the country does not realize the immense amount of money it costs us yearly to maintain that railroad. It is the custom to charge the deficit of the Intercolonial Railway in this manner, but it is a wrong principle. Until the country knows exactly what this railroad is costing them, and until the government realize their responsibility and operate this railroad in a business like manner, the present condition of things is likely to continue.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Haggart) takes the capital. expenditure and deficit for the year and charges and treats it all as the deficit of the year. I think he is unreasonable. The money charged to capital account, if properly applied, always1 goes to the betterment of the property, and the interest on capital expenditure is a legitimate charge on the year's operations, but to charge the whole of the year's capital to the deficit account is a method of calculation that my hon. friend (Mr. Haggart) would not like to have bad applied in his day.

Mr. Alexander Mackenzie when Minister of Railways said that the Intercolonial Railway was a completed undertaking, and that the capital account should have ceased altogether. That is my argument, and my statement is that the capital account or whatever you call it is expended on the railroad for the year, and in that way there is over .$8,000,000 taken out of the pockets of the people of the country this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When my hon. friend takes the deficit for the year and adds that to the capital expenditure for the year, he is unfair. The money expended on capital, assuming it is properly applied, goes to the betterment of the property and you only have the right to charge the interest on that capital to the annual output.
My hon. friend (Mr. Haggart) was taking the capital account and he was adding to that the deficit which must be paid from some source, and
lie said the Intercolonial Railway cost the people of this country that much more than the people receive out of it. The Minister of Finance says that we should not charge the deficit to capital.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You should not charge the capital with the deficit.
What will you do with the deficit ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You have to pay it out of the general revenue of Canada.

Suppose a private corporation were operating a railroad and there was a deficit of $1,000,000 a year, and you had deficits of this kind accumulating year after year ; in the end that must be met by a fresh supply of capital or you must close up your railroad. It seems to me that the deficits on the Intercolonial Railway as on any other railroad must in the end be paid out of capital. The Minister of Finance says we have not added the deficit, to capital from year to year.
As a matter of fact we have.
The Minister of Finance says not.
I say we have.

I am assuming for the purposes of argument that we have not. It seems to me that that only makes the conditions worse, because while we have $70,000,000 of capital account, in order to get the true position of affairs we should have added to that year after year the deficit, which if this railroad were owned by a corporation would have to be added to capitalization or provided for in some way.
I do not know much about railway accounts, but I think that is common sense. While we must accept the statement of the Minister of Railways as to some of the causes which in his opinion have led to this extraordinary result during the past year, it seems to me that the hon. minister did not give any satisfactory explanation as to why there is so remarkable a difference between the results of the operation of this railway and the results of the operation of the other great railways in Canada. I understand that the percentage of expenditure to receipts on these other railways is from 65 to 70 per cent while on the Intercolonial Railway the percentage of expenditure to receipts is 110 to 115 per cent. That is a very remarkable difference. We know that some peculiar conditions have to be taken into consideration in connection with the Intercolonial Railway.
We know that the Intercolonial Railway competes with water carriage more than any other railway in Canada; we know it runs through a portion of country in the provinces of New Brunswick and Quebec, which is not very thickly settled; but outside of these reasons and the low rates
which were mentioned by the Minister of Railways, I do not know of any reason which should operate to make the results
so very different. It is remarkable that from 05 to 72 per cent of the gross earnings are sufficient to operate railways in other parts of Canada, and even in the same portions of Canada, while in the case of the Intercolonial it takes 110 or 115 per cent of the gross earnings. What is the reason for that? Is there not some other reason than what the hon. Minister of Railways has given us to-day ? My right hon. friend the Prime Minister declared in a speech within the past fifteen or eighteen months that the whole system was vicious. The Minister of Railways seems to have given very good evidence to-night that there is something wrong about the system, otherwise he would have been able to have set forth a different result from what he did. If the system is vicious and brings about such an extraordinary result as he has presented, how is it that we do not hear from the government some statement of the particulars in which it is vicious and some proposal or policy by means of which that vicious system can be modified so as to become at least less vicious and produce better results? There is no use of calling on the House and the country year afteryear for a million or a million and a half to pay off a deficit, or for three or four millions to be spent on a capital account that should have been closed long ago, and saying without any explanation that the whole thing is vicious. There is not much logic or reason or statesmanship about that.

The Finance Minister says that expenditure on capital account on the Intercolonial Railway should be charged to capital, and that only the interest should be charged against revenue. That would be all very well if there were a profit from the expenditure of capital. The Minister of Railways told us to-night in his very lucid speech that we had come to the point where we must realize that the Intercolonial Railway must be operated at a loss. That being the case, do not let us deceive ourselves, but let us boldly face the met aud let the people of this country realize that all the expenditure on the Intercolonial Railway is practically a charge against the revenue of this country. The Intercolonial has been in operation as a finished road for the greater part of twenty

five years. It is quite true that during the first ten or fifteen years in the life of a railway, expenditures for renewals, increased sidings, &c., are charged pretty much against capital. But having taken two trips over the Intercolonial last summer, I think the roadbed, the rolling stock and the railway generally is in a first-class condition.
Therefore there should not be any necessity for an expenditure exceeding the ordinary expenditure on a completed railway. Very few of the items now charged to capital account on the Intercolonial Railway would be charged to capital account by any ordinary railway company. We are deceiving ourselves by adding year after year $3,000,000, $4,000,000, $5,000,000 to capital account, on which there is no apparent possibility of our obtaining any returns. Therefore that money should be charged, not to capital, but to revenue, because it Is so much less in the operation of the railroad. The extraordinary thing to my mind is that item after item Is for extensions of sidings and extensions of accommodations, and yet, according to the minister's own statement, the gross earnings for this current year are not greater than they were two or three years ago. That is something no one can understand. The Intercolonial Railway is doing a large business, it is participating in the increased business all over the country, and as is has not, according to the hon. minister, changed its rates for passengers or freight it ought, in the ordinary course of things, to have received a very much larger gross icvenue this year than it did the year previous. That is quite apart from the increased expenditure. But if you take the trouble to look over the items charged to capital account in the public accounts in 1904, you will see how utterly absurd they are, especially on a road which is not doing, according to the minister's statement, any increased business. The statement of the minister can have only one meaning, and that is that the business on the road to-day is not greater than it was two years ago, and yet an enormous sum has been expended the last two years on rolling stock and on renewals of rolling stock, so that the road ought to have a very ample supply of rolling stock for its business. Take item after item in this long list of expenditures charged to capital account, and you will find such items as increased accommodation at small stations, $662.57, siding to wharf at Campbeliton, $1,250. Although there is no increase in business, these little sidings here and there are charged to capital account. Then there is a new freight shed $1,228, dwelling for agent $1,699 and freight house $1,300 charged to capital account, and these on a road which has been in operation for 34 or 35 years and has been a finished road for 25 or 30 years. No private corporation would dream of charging these items to capital account.

When a road has been put in first-class order, when all its bridges and other permanent structures are completed, there is no charge for maintenance or renewal added to capital account. He should let the people know exactly what that new road is going to cost. Taking the statement of the Minister of Railways that we cannot expect anything but deficits on the Intercolonial Railway in the future, we are simply attempting to deceive ourselves when we do not charge the whole amount expended on the Intercolonial to revenue.

I would like to recall to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance the argument he was so ready with two or three years ago, when, in this House, I called attention to the very objectionable system of the government of charging the renewal of rails to capital account. What did the hon. gentleman say ? He said : Oh, what difference does it make whether you charge it to capital or working expenses, the country has to pay all the same. If that be so, if the capital expenditure plus the deficit goes to the general debt of the country, what is the use of finessing about whether it is correct to make the charge to capital account or not. It is quite true the deficit is not charged to the capital of the Intercolonial Railway, but the debt of this country to-day is so much greater by the deficits on the Intercolonial Railway. During this administration, the Intercolonial Railway has run short ,by nearly $8,000,000, including the present year. Does the hon. gentleman mean to say for a moment that our national debt is not thereby so much increased ? That I take to be practically what the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) means, and the people do not seem to understand that our deficits on the Intercolonial Railway are running up the debt of this country. The hon. gentleman speaks as if calling the loss a deficit, wipes it off. But somebody has to pay the money; it must come out of the pockets of the people; it is added to the debt of the country. What is the position in the year reported upon in the Blue-book before us ?
The Minister of Railways, who thinks he has made a most satisfactory report, lias paid $114 to earn every hundred dollars we got in, and according to him that is satisfactory. If that W'ere satisfactory to him in his own personal affairs, he would soon be wound up. No man- is able to pay $114 out of $100 by any process I have ever learned unless he goes into debt, and this country goes into debt every year it has a deficit. Of that there can be no question. The Finance Minister may say that the capital account of the Intercolonial Railway is not added to by these deficits. That is quite true. We find at page ii 32 the whole thing set forth, and you find millions upon millions added from year to year to capital expenditure and in another column the deficits, but they all come out of the same pot and the country has to foot the Bill. Whether you call it technically capital account or not, the country has to pay it. Wliat my hon. friend means is that the people ought to understand that.
Three years ago I argued that very large sums improperly charged to capital should be charged to revenue and that there should be no concealment of the real loss on working by turning over to capital account But tiie lion, gentleman wanted a surplus on these occasions. He was then congratulating the country that in every line of our public finances there was a surplus. His surpluses were made out of deficits. He had a deficit on the Intercolonial, but he charged it up to another account, to capital, and, having pulled out the plum of a surplus in this way, he said : ' What a good boy am i ! He simply ran the country into debt ; and then he said : ' What difference does it make whether you charge it to capital or anything else, for the country has to pay it just the same ? And the Minister of Finance knows it as well as I do, and I defy him to say that he does not. He knew that the system pursued by the ex-Minister of Railways was wrong. I want to say a word about the Question of capital account. The hon. gentleman seems to be surprised that there should be any recognized principle about a going concern finding whatever^ is necessary to carry on its business. The recognized principle is, and you will find it laid down in Adam's work, that a going concern has to provide without adding to its cost or its capital whatever may be necessary for its business from time to time. The principle is exactly the same as that which applies to a merchant or a manufacturer who wants to make some improvement about his premises. For instance, a merchant might want to put in plate glass windows. He does make a mortgage to pay for them or add them to the cost of his establishment. His business warrants the improvement and he puts plate glass windows in because the improvement is going to pay him and he is going to get a revenue immediately from it. That is the principle which must be applied. You must not add to your capital account. It is a check upon keeping your improvements in step with your business. The difficulty about that has arisen in this way: A very large number of railway companies found, when they wanted to put in heavier rails or get heavier locomotives or whatever the business at that time warranted, that they had not the money and these railway companies had to put a capital mortgage on their property. So, they did things which were contrary to the true principle-I can give the hon. gentleman the authority for it-which is that a going concern must maintain itself and keep up with the business of the times, and if it cannot do that it should show by its revenue accounts that it is losing and not cover it up.

My hon. friend (Mr. Osier) said that this was a finished concern; that its earning power was at a standstill and that therefore we should close the capital account-

The railway report shows that there was a decrease in gross earnings last year as compared with the year before.
Mr. EMMERSON My hon. friend is entirely wrong. An increase in gross earnings is shown by the report, and it is estimated that this year the increase will be $419,474.
Do you not see that if you pay $114 to earn $100, the greater the gross earnings the more you will lose ?
That is another question altogether. It was stated here that the gross earnings of the Intercolonial Railway were not increasing, and I have shown by the figures that that statement is erroneous.
What I said was that the net earnings were growing worse from year to year. There was nearly $1,000,000 short last year, and the minister tells us that this year there will be $2,000,000 short.

My hon friend from Toronto (Mr. Osier) and my hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Haggart) made the positive statement that although we had extended the railway, the business had not increased. I have shown that that statement is wrong. Furthermore, if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Haggart) looks at the figures he will find that in the capital expenditure of the Intercolonial Railway last year is included $800,000 for the acquisition of the Canada Eastern, and that fact he has ignored. The other expenditures charged to capital account last year were for extensions to the road, improvements, betterments, double tracking at different points, and the strengthening of the bridges on the Drummond County section which are not adapted for the passage of the very heavy engines used at the present day. If the cost of management of the Intercolonial is only to be computed upon the basis of capital expenditure, I think it is only a fair proposition that the same method should be applied to the canals. The people of the
country want to know what the Intercolonial is costing them by way of capital and other expenditure. They also want to know what their canal system is costing them. I think we should look at this matter fairly. The Intercolonial has many burdens ; but it is doing and has done a great work in connection with the building up of this country. It is a splendid road, and it is kept in condition. I think the conditions prevailing on the Intercolonial to-day are such that no man will say that there is a better road anywhere in America. Its train service is modern and up-to-date, and its roadbed is in splendid repair.

I would like to ask a question of the hon. member for Hamilton in reference to capital account. Suppose a mine were discovered on the line of the Intercolonial, and a town sprung up there suddenly, and the management came to the conclusion that it would be necessary to construct a new railway station there, and also a hotel costing say $500,000. We understand that the Grand Trunk Railway Company, now that they are taking over the Canada Atlantic, propose to build a new railway station and a hotel in Ottawa. Would not these two items be properly charged to capital account ?

With regard to the hotel, we might perhaps go into the question whether or not the hon. gentleman would allow me to /sell whisky and a number of other things. With regard to the new station, I would say that, on the principle on which all such accounts are kept, if there were business forthcoming from that time that would justify the building of the station, then the station should be built and the revenue from the mine should pay for it.

I am not asking
what should pay for it. I am asking whether that should be charged to capital account or not ?

No, it should not. It is a strict rule that a going concern maintains itself. The principle is that the going concern adds to its facilities according to the business it sees before it from these improvements, just as my hon. friend would in carrying on his business as ia merchant..
On this item of the Murray Harbour branch and the Hillsboro' Bridge, the minister promised to bring down the contract and some other things.
I think the papers were all brought down.
We have not received any notice of the papers having been brought down up to the present time. I do not think we can very well proceed with this item until they are brought down.

The minister is in error. I asked for papers with regard to

railway extensions in the province and also for papers in regard to expenditures on railways and canals in Canada, and these have not been brought down.
I think the hon. minister must have them in his desk, as the clerk of the House has not received them yet.
Instructions were given to have all that information prepared, and I was under the impression that it was brought down. I shall certainly have it prepared for my hon. friend.

Before the item passes we would like to know what the minister is doing with regard to railway extension in the province. With regard to surveys from Stanley bridge, I think there are some in the department, but would like to know what the government propose doing ? There are also in the department, as the minister knows, some claims for damages sustained by pai'ties in connection with those surveys, and the papers with regard to these ought to be laid on the table.
Does my hon. friend mean the papers relating to the land damage claims ?

l'es. The minister knows that some demands have been made on him which the department very unfairly refused to pay, and there is a report of his own engineer in his department which gives some information in regard to them.
I would like to see those papers.
I do not think it has a bearing on this at all. That is on the Murray Harbour branch ?
No, on the Stanley and New London branch.
We will have an opportunity of discnssing it on the supplementary estimates.

I would suggest that as the information promised is now down,, we should let this item stand until the sup-plementaries are down. ^
Mr. EMMERSON You could pass it now and discuss it then.
Will the hon. gentleman give us the assurance that there will he some items in the supplementaries on those lines ?
I can say that to my hon. friend.

On the 13th March there was an order of the House for eopies of all correspondence, &c., relating to land damages claimed on account of lands expropriated on the Murray harbour branch of the Prince Edward Island Railway. That has not been brought down. We were also promised the contract between the goy-

eminent and the contractor and we have not yet got It. This item cannot be intelligently discussed until that information is before us.	.

As the papers are not down, it would be perhaps better to
take this item up with the supplementaries.
There will be an item in the supplementaries on this very matter when the whole item can be discussed.
When will the supple-mentaries be brought down ?
Some time next week-
I think we are justified in insisting that the papers should be down before we pass this item.

I have no desire to prevent discussion and only suggest that, in order to expedite business, we should pass it now, and discuss it later on in the supplementaries. My hon. friends will then have no cause to complain of lack of information.

The other course would he more desirable and there will be no time lost.
Item allowed to stand.
National Transcontinental Railway-surveys, construction and other expenses, $1,328,500.
There was a map brought down which partly explains what surveys have been made, but we have no report of the expenditure.
That is all contained in the report of the commission.
Is there any information in it in reference to gradients and curvatures ?
It has very full information.
I have never received any copy.
It was laid on the table three weeks ago and ordered to be printed immediately and ought to be here now. I cannot understand why it is not.

The minister will see we cannot discuss this without any information. But if the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) wishes it, we could make an arrangement under which this matter could be discussed on an item in the supplementary estimates. Is that satisfactory?

Yes, so far as I am concerned ; but I do not wish to press it upon any other hon. member. The only conditions I would make are that we shall have the printing expedited-the printed copies should have been in our hands long

ago-and that the supplementary vote to which reference has been made shall be brought up at a reasonably early date. With that undei'standing, we can pass this item.
Mr. EM ME It SOX. Do I understand that objection is taken to item 87?

Yes, that item stands.
Public Works-chargeable to income-harbours and rivers-New Brunswick-Cape Tor-mentine-improvements and repairs to harbour works, $22,000.
Mr. BRODET'R. This vote is to provide for works required to make good the damage done by the teredo, the harbour works having been greatly weakened by that destructive sea worm. This work is in Westmoreland county.

I understand that a great deal of money is spent every year on this work, as the storms are very heavy and the waves break over this work. It is stated that the work is not rip-rap. It is open to the storms and in the first storm of the autumn some portion is apt to be carried away. It is contended that it is absolutely necessary that this should be rip-rapped with heavy stone.
That is what is being done by the department, as it has been found that the work done hitherto is not satisfactory.
Has a contract been let for this?

No, it is done by day's work.
Chance harbour-'breakwater, $1,000.
Mr. BRODEUR This work is in the county of St. John. The item is a revote to provide for the completion of a small submerged breakwater. The estimated expenditure on the work is $4,000.
Will the work be completed tliis season?

Yes, it is hoped so.
Clifton (Stonehaven)-breakwater-improvements and repairs, $9,000.
This is for maintenance.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
That can hardly be, for only $2,500 was voted last year, whereas $9,000 is asked this year.	.
Mr. BRODEUR, It is intended to render the harbour more secure and to prevent the waves bringing in sand and filling in the harbour and reducing its depth. The total cost will be $9,000 according to the estimate of the engineer.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Is this being done by contract?
Mr. BRODEUR, No, by day's work.
Dipper harbour-breakwater, $35,000.
This is under contract.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Will this complete the work?
Mr. BRODEUR, This sum of money wifi complete it. But it may not all be spent this season.
What is the total cost?
The estimate is $48,000.
How much was expended last year ?
Three thousand dollars. It is estimated that $33,000 will be spent before the end of the fiscal year. This work is in the county of St. John.
I suppose there have been some changes during the last year that increased the estimate. I noticed in the discussion of the item last year the minister stated that the total cost would be $30,000.

I am informed that new plans have been made.
-Mr. BLAIN. I would regard that as lather unusual, that the estimated cost was $30,000 as stated last year, and then the following year new plans are prepared increasing the amount to $4S,000.

Tenders were called for o:i the original plans and none came in ; so the plans had to be changed and new tenders asked for.
Durham-wharf, $15,000.

Tenders have been called for and received, but the contract is not yet awarded. This estimate is for a wharf to be built at the eastern end of the parish of Durham, which will give a depth of six feet in low water and fifteen feet in high water. It is a new wharf.
Great Salmon river-groyne and breakwater combined, $4,300.

This is also in the comity of St. John. Some tenders were called for but none were received, and we will have to call for new tenders. Nothing has been spent during the past year.
Miscou harbour-wharf, $S,000.

This is under contract, in Gloucester county. 'The contractors are Messrs. Burns and Charleson. It is a new wharf. There are about 70 bouses on tlie Island including 11 lobster factories, two of which are engaged also in canning salmon. The population is estimated at about 500. The occupation of t'he people is mainly fishing for lobsters, herring, salmon and smelts. Farming is carried on to some extent.
The lobster factories are mere sbeds. fi'he whole bunch of them
would not be worth $2,000, and you are sitending $16,000 for a wharf to accommodate about 50 houses.

If the hon. gentleman lived on the north shore he might change his opinion. The lobster factories there represent a large amount of capital, thousands of dollars are invested in each one of them. There is an immense trade in bringing provisions to these factories, but they are without any shipping facilities.
How many months in the year are they in operation ?
How long has all this been going on ?
For years and years. Unfortunately the government has neglected those people.
I can tell the hon. gen-jfclejman that all the exports he is talking about do not amount to $75,000, and the imports only amount to $50,000.
I cannot give the figures, but I know7 there is an immense trade done there which requires these facilities.
The contract price is $13,700. Why are you increasing that amount ?
1 am not asking for a larger amount. The contract is for $13,700, but there is superintendence and contingencies in connection wdth the execution of the contract, which raise the amount to $15,000.
______Would the minister excuse me for going back to the Salmon river item, and tell me when are these tenders to be called for.
They will be called for as soon as possible, this season.
I suppose the minister is aware that the mill property at Salmon river is owned by a private corporation. Are there any people living there except those who are working for this corporation ?
This is a public work.
I say there are no people served except the people of this corporation. I know7 the property very well. It is a mill property and it is owned by an American corporation.
It belongs now to the government.

I am speaking of this place, Salmon river. There is no public interest, but that of the people w7ho are engaged by this corporation. The facilities you put there will simply be for the advantage of this corporation.
This corporation exports a good deal of lumber, does it not ?
I say that. Does this property belong to the government ?

It belongs to the government.

This is for a small eribwork and breakwater 80 feet long which it has been decided to build at Mud Cove on Grindstone Island at the head of the Bay of Fundy.
How much was expended last year ?

speechtext: This is $1,000 of a revote ?
Yes.

In King's and Albert county.

At Grindstone Island which is 30 miles long and a quarter of a mile w7ide.

This is under contract.
What is the amount of the contract ?
Will that complete the work?
first cost of wharfs built by them in tidal waters, $5,000.

I would like to say in connection with this item that it does seem to me that the time has arrived when the Dominion government should pay the whole of the cost of these wharfs. The finances of the province are not in a healthy condition and the total cost 'of works of this character constructed in other provinces is paid for by the Dominion government. I think that New Brunswick should be placed on the same footing as other provinces in respect to this matter. It is very important to navigation that you should supply these facilities to the people along the St. John river. This is just as important as it is to build a wharf at Miscou where this lobster 'industry is carried on. The St. John river is the highway of commerce running through the centre of the province of New Brunswick and, I do think the Dominion government should defray the whole cost of these wharfs instead of compelling the local government ; which is very ill able to do it, to pay half the cost.
I understand that is in virtue of an agreement between the local and federal governments. I suppose the agreement will have to be carried out until it is changed.

I might relieve the mind of the minister by saying that I have not the slightest doubt tfle local government would be perfectly willing to cancel tlie\ agreement if the Dominion government would take on itself the burden of providing the whole cost. I know this custom has existed for many years, but there always comes a time when it is well to change, and it seems to me the Dominion government should now consider whether they will not provide the whole cost of these different constructions along the St. John river.

That might be discussed when we are considering the relations between the Dominion and the provinces.
St. John harbour-repairs and extension ol protection work at base of Fort Dufferin, $500.
Is this, an annual vote ?
No.

The timber decays and has to be renewed.
Could it not he built of stone and made permanent ?
